title: The Ice Pop Stand
sum: Rosa and her little brother Nico sell homemade ice pops on hot summer days to buy a new sprinkler.

cast.d: a six-year-old girl who wants a new sprinkler for the hot summer
cast.look: a six-year-old girl with two curly dark puffs of hair, a green T-shirt and a big straw sun hat

cast.d: Rosa's four-year-old brother, who always wants a taste
cast.look: a four-year-old boy with a round face, red shorts and a T-shirt with juice spots

cast.d: Rosa and Nico's aunt, who has the freezer and the ice pop tray
cast.look: a tall woman with short gray hair, round glasses and a yellow apron

cast.d: Aunt Bea's old dog, who always finds the shade
cast.look: an old brown dog with floppy ears and a gray chin

cast.d: the mail carrier, the stand's first and last customer
cast.look: a mail carrier in a blue uniform and a blue cap, with a big mail bag

cast.d: the owner of the hardware store that sells the sprinkler
cast.look: a man with a gray mustache and a red store vest

p: It was the hottest day of the summer. The sidewalk was too hot for bare feet. Biscuit, Aunt Bea's old brown dog, lay flat under the porch and panted.
“Sprinkler time!” said Nico. He was four, and he loved the sprinkler more than cake. Aunt Bea turned on the tap.
The old green sprinkler coughed. Pfft. Pfft. Then it gave one sad little drip.
Aunt Bea picked it up and turned it over. A long crack ran down one side. “It's broken,” she said. “A new one costs ten dollars.”
Rosa checked her pockets. She found a pebble and a string. No dollars. Nico flopped on the grass like a starfish.
Aunt Bea fanned her face with her hat. “What does everybody want on a day like this?” “Something cold,” said Rosa. “Ice pops!” yelled Nico.
Aunt Bea snapped her fingers. “Then let's sell ice pops. One dollar for one pop.” Rosa grabbed Nico's hands, and they spun in a circle. They could buy the new sprinkler themselves!
In the kitchen, Aunt Bea took down a plastic tray. It had two rows of little molds, five in each row. Ten molds and ten wooden sticks.
First came the strawberry juice, red as a fire truck. Glug, glug. Rosa filled four molds.
Next came the orange juice. Nico held the tray still, with his tongue poking out. Three more molds were full.
Then came the grape juice, dark and purple. It filled two molds. The bottle gave a hollow gurgle. Empty!
Nico counted the full molds with one finger. “One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine.” His finger stopped over the last mold. It was still dry.
“We need more juice,” said Rosa. She opened the fridge. Milk, eggs, pickles. Then she spotted two yellow lemons in the back.
Aunt Bea cut the lemons and squeezed them into a cup. Nico licked a drop off his thumb. His whole face scrunched up like a raisin. “Sour!”
Aunt Bea stirred in cold water and a big spoon of sugar. Rosa took a sip. Sour first, then sweet. She poured it into the last mold.
Every mold was full now. The juice sloshed when Aunt Bea lifted the tray. It was still runny.
Aunt Bea slid the tray into the freezer. A puff of cold air made Rosa shiver. “It's very cold in there,” she said. “By morning, that juice will be ice.”
At bedtime, Rosa peeked in. The pops were hard around the edges but soft on top, like slush. She shut the door fast.
In the morning, Rosa ran straight to the freezer. She tapped a red pop with one finger. Tap, tap. Hard as a rock!
Next, she made a sign out of cardboard. She wrote ICE POPS in tall black letters. Under that, she wrote ONE DOLLAR.
Nico drew a sun in the corner. It had a big smile and three drops of sweat. “It's hot,” he said. “Just like me.”

art.s: In a sunny kitchen, Rosa and her little brother Nico pour red, orange and purple juice into a tray of ten ice pop molds while Aunt Bea squeezes a lemon.

q.q: Draw the juice going into the freezer, then the pops coming out. What changed?
look: runny juice in the molds before
hard ice pops after the freezer
q.e: Yes! The cold freezer turned runny juice into hard ice.

q.q: Nico tasted the lemon juice. What word did he say?
q.e: Lemons taste sour. That is why Nico's face scrunched up like a raisin.

q.q: The tray had ten molds. Nine were full. How many more did they need?
q.e: Nine and one more make ten. The lemon juice filled the last mold.

p: The ice pop stand opened at ten o'clock. Rosa and Nico dragged a little table out to the sidewalk. Aunt Bea brought two chairs and an empty jar.
Rosa taped the sign to the front of the table. ICE POPS, ONE DOLLAR. On the jar, she wrote SPRINKLER. A new one cost ten dollars.
Nico laid all the pops on a big white plate. Four red, three orange, two purple and one yellow. They shone like jewels in the sun.
It was already hot. The sun beat down on the table. Biscuit stayed on the porch, in the shade.
The first customer was Ms. Kim, the mail carrier. Her face was pink and shiny. “Whew! One red one, please,” she said. She tucked a dollar into the jar.
Then a boy on a scooter zipped up. He picked an orange pop and paid with a crumpled dollar. Off he zoomed, licking.
Nico poked the purple pop. “Hey! It's sweating!” Tiny drops ran down its sides. Drip. Drip. Drip.
A purple puddle spread across the plate. The yellow pop bent on its stick like a sleepy flower. Rosa's stomach dropped. The pops were melting!
“I can help,” said Nico. He licked the purple drips off the plate. Then the drips on his wrist. Then the drips on his chin.
Rosa put her hand flat on the table. The sunny part was hot, like a slide in summer. She reached under the table, into the shade. It was cool down there.
She slid the plate under the table, out of the sun. The drips came slower now. Drip… drip.
Aunt Bea came out and saw the purple puddle. “Ice pops don't like the sun,” she said. “The sun warms them up, and warm ice turns back into juice. Like a snowman in spring.”
She ran inside and came back with the blue cooler. It was full of ice cubes. Rosa tucked the pops inside, and the lid shut with a thunk.
The two purple pops were too soft to sell. Aunt Bea slid them off their sticks into a cup. Nico drank the purple juice in one long slurp.
Later, two girls walked by from the library. Their cheeks were red from the heat. Rosa opened the cooler, and cold air puffed out. The red pops were still hard.
“Two red ones, please,” said the tall girl. They each paid one dollar. Crunch! went the first bite.
At five o'clock, Rosa tipped out the jar and counted the dollars. Nico counted too. He counted the purple spots on his shirt.
He had more spots than dollars. He grinned up at Rosa. Even his teeth were purple.

art.s: Rosa and Nico sit at a small ice pop stand on a sunny sidewalk while purple juice drips from a plate of melting ice pops.

q.q: Draw the jar with all the dollars from today. How many did they get?
q.e: Ms. Kim, the boy on the scooter and two girls. That makes four dollars!

q.q: Where did the pops melt faster, in the sun or in the shade?
q.e: The sun warmed the pops, so they dripped fast. In the shade, the drips came slower.

q.q: Which sound did the melting pops make?
q.e: Drip, drip! Melting ice makes little drops of juice.

p: The next morning, Rosa had a plan. “No more sun on the pops,” she said. “Today we sit in the shade.”
A big oak tree grew in front of Aunt Bea's house. Its shade lay across the whole sidewalk, dark and cool. Rosa and Nico set up the table right in the middle of it.
The blue cooler went under the table. The jar went on top, with four dollars from yesterday. The new sprinkler cost ten.
Nico found his shadow on the grass. It was long and skinny, with very long legs. “Look!” he said. “I'm taller than Aunt Bea!”
A jogger stopped at the stand, puffing hard. He bought an orange pop and ate it in four bites. Crunch, crunch, crunch, crunch.
All morning, the shade crept across the sidewalk, bit by bit. It was as quiet as a cat. Nobody noticed.
By lunchtime, the back of Rosa's neck felt hot. She looked up. The table was in bright sun again! The shade had slid away toward the fence.
“Who moved the shade?” said Rosa. Nico looked for his shadow. It was a little dark blob by his shoes. “My shadow is hiding!” he said.
Aunt Bea pointed up. The sun was high over the tree now. “The sun moves across the sky all day,” she said. “So the shade moves too.”
“Then we move too!” said Rosa. She grabbed one end of the table. Nico grabbed the other end. Mostly, he just hung on.
They dragged the table into the new shade. One big step. Two big steps. Three big steps. Scrape, scrape, scrape.
The cool shade covered the table again. Biscuit trotted over and flopped down right under it. “Biscuit knew all along,” said Aunt Bea. “He follows the shade every day.”
After lunch, a woman came by with a baby in a stroller. The baby pointed at the red pop and squealed. The woman laughed and bought it.
Then old Mr. Hill from next door shuffled over in his slippers. He looked at the yellow pop for a long time. Then he picked an orange one.
“Nobody ever picks the yellow one,” Nico whispered. Rosa shrugged. The yellow one was lemon, and lemon was sour.
By five o'clock, the shade stretched far across the yard. Nico's shadow had long legs again. He danced, and his shadow danced too.
Rosa counted the jar. Four old dollars and three new ones made seven. “Seven!” Nico told his shadow. His shadow waved back.

art.s: Rosa and Nico drag a small ice pop table across the sidewalk into the shade of a big oak tree while an old brown dog naps under it.

q.q: How many big steps did they drag the table into the shade?
q.e: One, two, three big steps, right into the cool shade.

q.q: Draw Nico at lunchtime, looking for his shadow. How does his face look?
look: Nico looking down at his shoes
a tiny shadow by his feet
q.e: Great picture! We can see Nico's surprise on his face.

q.q: Why did the shade move away from the table?
c: The sun moved across the sky.
The wind blew the shade away.
q.e: The sun moved across the sky, so the tree's shade moved too.

p: The next morning, Rosa opened the freezer. It was almost empty. Only one pop was left, and it was the yellow one.
“The yellow one again,” said Nico. Rosa looked at the jar on the counter. Seven dollars. The new sprinkler cost ten.
“Let's make more pops,” said Rosa. But the juice was all gone. Aunt Bea shook the last bottle upside down. Not one drop came out.
Then Rosa spotted the watermelon on the counter. It was round and green and as big as a beach ball. Nico tried to lift it. His face went red, and the watermelon did not move.
“Could we make pops out of that?” asked Rosa. Aunt Bea took out her biggest knife. “Stand back,” she said.
Crack! The watermelon split in two. Juice ran across the cutting board and dripped onto the floor. Biscuit licked it up in two seconds.
Rosa leaned in close. The outside was dark green, with a white stripe under it. The inside was bright pink and dotted with black seeds.
“Why does it have seeds?” asked Nico. “Seeds are how a watermelon makes more watermelons,” said Aunt Bea. “Plant one, and a new vine can grow.” Nico's eyes went round.
Aunt Bea cut the pink part into chunks. Rosa and Nico picked out the seeds with their fingers. Plink, plink, into a bowl.
Some seeds were big and black. Others were small, white and soft. “The white ones never got big,” said Aunt Bea. “Only the black ones can grow.”
Next, Rosa mashed the chunks with a potato masher. Squish, squish. Soon the bowl was full of pink, lumpy juice. It smelled sweet and fresh.
Nico poured it into the molds. Only a little went on the floor. Biscuit took care of that too.
Aunt Bea slid the tray into the freezer. “Pops need a few hours to freeze,” she said. Nico sat down in front of the freezer door to wait.
So Aunt Bea gave him a job. She handed him a paper cup full of dirt. Nico poked a hole with his finger and dropped in one big black seed. He patted the dirt flat and gave it a drink of water.
He set the cup on the sunny windowsill. “Grow,” he told it. “Grow as big as a beach ball.”
By three o'clock, the pink pops were hard. Rosa and Nico carried the cooler out to the shade of the oak tree. The yellow pop came too, just in case.
Two kids rode up on bikes. Their helmets were crooked, and their faces were red. “Pink ones, please!” they said. Each one paid a dollar.
Nico held up the yellow pop. The kids shook their heads and rode away, licking. Rosa counted the jar twice. So close! Just one more dollar, and they would have ten.
That night, Nico checked his cup on the windowsill. Only dirt. “Tomorrow,” he whispered to it.

art.s: In a kitchen, Aunt Bea cuts a big watermelon while Rosa and Nico pick black seeds into a bowl and an old brown dog waits by their feet.

q.q: Draw Nico talking to his seed cup. Put his words in a speech bubble.
look: Nico next to a cup of dirt
q.e: Your speech bubble lets us hear Nico talk!

q.q: What can grow from a watermelon seed?
q.e: Seeds are how a watermelon makes more watermelons. Plant one, and a vine can grow.

q.q: The jar had seven dollars. Two kids paid one dollar each. How many now?
q.e: Seven, then eight, then nine. Just one more to make ten!

p: The next day was the hottest one yet. The jar held nine dollars. The new sprinkler cost ten. They needed one more dollar.
Rosa and Nico set up the stand under the oak tree. The cooler was full of pink watermelon pops. The yellow pop lay on top, same as always.
But the street was empty. No bikes, no strollers, no mail carrier. Even the birds were hiding in the trees.
An hour went by. Rosa's legs stuck to the chair. Nico lay on the grass next to Biscuit, and they both panted.
“Nobody knows we're here,” said Rosa. “We need a song!” She stood up tall and cupped her hands around her mouth.
“Ice pops, ice pops, cold and sweet!” she sang. “Come and get a frozen treat!”
Nico jumped up. “Pink ones, yellow ones, one for you! Come and get a pop or two!” Biscuit howled along. Aroo!
They sang it again, louder. A window opened across the street. Then a blue cap came around the corner. It was Ms. Kim, with her big mail bag.
“I heard a song about ice pops,” she said. Rosa lifted the cooler lid. “We have pink ones. They're watermelon.”
Ms. Kim peeked in. Then she pointed. “What about that yellow one?”
“That one is lemon,” said Nico. He scrunched up his face. “It's sour.” Ms. Kim clapped her hands. “Sour is my favorite!”
She took one big lick. Her lips puckered, and her eyes squeezed shut. “Mmm. Perfect.” Then she tucked a dollar into the jar.
Rosa counted every dollar out loud. Nico shouted the last number. “TEN!” Biscuit barked too.
They ran all the way to Mr. Ortiz's hardware store. Aunt Bea puffed along behind them. The new sprinkler sat in the window. It was blue, with a round middle and three long arms.
Rosa set the jar on the counter. Mr. Ortiz counted the dollars, all the way to ten. Then he handed Rosa the box. Now the jar was empty, and Rosa hugged the box all the way home.
Back home, Aunt Bea hooked up the hose and turned the tap. Whoosh! The arms spun, and water flew out in a big circle.
Nico ran through first. Then Rosa. Then Biscuit, snapping at every drop.
Suddenly Rosa stopped. There, in the spray, was a little rainbow! Red, orange, yellow, green, blue and purple.
“Where did that come from?” asked Nico. “The sun is behind you, shining into the water drops,” said Aunt Bea. “Sunlight has all those colors in it. The drops spread them out.”
Rosa peeked over her shoulder. There was the sun, right behind her. She could feel it, warm on her back.
Nico pointed at the stripes. “Red, orange, yellow, purple,” he said. “It's made of ice pops!” Then he ran through it again.

art.s: Rosa, Nico and an old brown dog run through a spinning blue sprinkler in a sunny yard while a small rainbow shines in the spray.

q.q: In Rosa's song, which word rhymes with sweet?
q.e: Sweet and treat! Rhyming words end with the same sound.

q.q: They paid all ten dollars for the sprinkler. How many were left in the jar?
q.e: Ten dollars went to Mr. Ortiz, so the jar was empty. Zero dollars, one new sprinkler!

q.q: Draw the sprinkler making a rainbow. Show where the sun is.
q.e: Sun behind you, water drops in front. That's how you find a rainbow!

fin.q: First they made pops. Next they sold them. What did they buy last?
fin.e: First, next, last! The ice pop money bought a new sprinkler.

fin.q: The freezer turned juice into ice. What turned the ice back into juice?
fin.e: The hot sun melted the pops. The cooler and the shade kept them hard.
